paras: The Ridgetop train hold-up took place on the night of August 29, 1903, when fifteen to twenty masked men stopped a Louisville & Nashville passenger train near Ridgetop, Tennessee, and searched it for Will Reed, a Black worker accused of shooting a construction foreman that day. Reed was not aboard, because officers had already taken him to Nashville by buggy, and a Kentucky paper judged that the band would otherwise have killed him.

Early on Saturday, August 29, Ollie Ware, a foreman or superintendent for the Mason-Hoge Company on the Louisville & Nashville tunnel through Baker's Hill, was shot at the construction camp. A Nashville special to the Louisville Courier-Journal said the quarrel "grew out of Ware's efforts to make the negro work," that Reed used a Winchester rifle and Ware a pistol, and that assistant superintendent Will Wheeler also fired at Reed without effect. Reed was captured that afternoon a few miles east of Springfield and carried to Nashville in a buggy.

That night the masked men signaled the engineer of the Nashville-bound train to stop at Ridgetop Station, near the construction camp. Most carried rifles and wore handkerchiefs over their faces up to their eyes, and they passed through every coach scrutinizing the passengers. Finding no sign of Reed, they left as quietly as they had come, and the train went on to Nashville after a delay of a few minutes, with no passenger harmed.

According to a report from his home in Louisa County, Virginia, Ware died the evening of the shooting, and his body was brought home on September 1. The same report said Reed had been lodged in the Nashville jail, that the affair "caused a great deal of excitement in Nashville," and that Reed would "have a speedy trial." No report of a trial, of any arrest of the masked men, or of an official response to the hold-up was found.

Only white newspapers carried the episode, and no Black-press coverage was found. The Hopkinsville Kentuckian, on the line the train had come from, gave the fullest account under the headline "Masked Men Hold Up Train, But Passengers Not Molested," and closed by calling it "very fortunate for Reed" that he had not been put on the train. A brief Nashville dispatch headed "Held Up a Train" and subtitled "Masked Men in Search of Supt. Ware's Slayer" ran in at least six Mississippi weeklies between September 3 and 5, often amid returns from the state's Democratic primary.

Papers in Ware's home state told a different story, headlined "Louisa Man Murdered," which praised Ware as "quiet, sober and industrious," called Reed "the negro murderer," and did not mention the masked band. None of the papers commented on the band's action or named any of its members.

Accounts of the quarrel differ: the Nashville special attributed it to Ware's attempt to make Reed work, while the Virginia report said Ware was killed by a worker "whom he had discharged." Both versions come from white sources, and no account from Reed or other workers appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Ridgetop train hold-up
bases: An armed, masked band stopped and searched a passenger train for a Black man accused of shooting a foreman, and a Kentucky paper judged they would have 'made short work of him' had he been aboard, an attempted lynching that failed because he was already in officers' hands (A2, A3).

The Hopkinsville Kentuckian's account and the separate Nashville wire dispatch agree on a masked band of fifteen to twenty men stopping the train at Ridgetop and searching it for Will Reed (A2, A3); the shooting itself is independently reported from Nashville and Virginia (A1, A5).

accounts.label: Nashville special to the Courier-Journal
accounts.gist: The row grew out of Ware's efforts to make Reed work; Reed fired a Winchester, Ware his pistol, and assistant superintendent Wheeler also fired; Reed was captured that afternoon.

accounts.label: Hopkinsville Kentuckian
accounts.gist: About twenty masked men with rifles quietly searched train No. 51 near Ridgetop for Reed, who had already been taken to Nashville by buggy; the paper judged he would have been killed had he been aboard.

accounts.label: Nashville wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Fifteen or twenty masked men signaled the Nashville-bound train to stop at Ridgetop Station, scrutinized every passenger, and failed to find Reed.

accounts.label: Virginia hometown report
accounts.gist: Ware was killed by a Black worker he had discharged, died the same evening, and his slayer was jailed in Nashville to await a speedy trial.

framing.detail: The Hopkinsville Kentuckian headlined 'MASKED MEN Hold Up Train, But Passengers Not Molested' and remarked it was 'very fortunate for Reed' he was not aboard, without comment on the band itself.
Mississippi weeklies ran the Nashville dispatch 'HELD UP A TRAIN' with the subhead 'Masked Men in Search of Supt. Ware's Slayer', treating Reed's guilt as settled.
Virginia papers headlined 'LOUISA MAN MURDERED', called Reed 'the negro murderer', praised Ware as 'quiet, sober and industrious', and did not mention the masked band.
